rv.q: But this overlong show stretches its razzing-the-wokerati joke so thin that there’s nothing substantial left to stand on by the time the authors truly have something to say.
Deep in Irony Spirals, Slam Frank Struggles to Show Its Core
This bizarre, uproariously funny and sharp-edged cartoon of a show was inspired by a 2022. Twitter debate which started with the horrifying premise, “Did Anne Frank have white privilege?”

As far as Hamilton knockoffs go—and there are a lot these days—Fox has actually written one of the better ones, with clever lyrics and catchy tunes ( Suffs, Pippin, and Cabaret also get their fair share of sampling).
Sam Lafrage’s direction can’t obscure some of the show’s early book problems.

This new musical by the clever pair of Andrew Fox (music and Lyrics) and Joel Sinensky (book) takes on many of the buzz words and hot topics of the 21 st century in what seems like a full-length Saturday Night Live skit intended to either include or insult everybody (take your pick.)
The premise is appropriately ridiculous but it can only carry the show so far.
There are some genuine moments of brilliance, such as Edith’s slam poem, “Yeast of Edith.”
Messrs. Fox and Sinensky, in contrast, press buttons to provoke and please modern audiences without really saying or doing anything original.

But while barreling forward through nearly two hours of song-and-dance-and-derision without let-up (or intermission), the show feels less and less entertaining, and the point of it all seems more and more uncertain.
It should unsettle you and entertain you in the same breath, and make you think while you're still laughing.
The jaw-dropping absurdity will continue to tickle your funny bone at the same time you tilt your head, asking yourself, WTF?!
Slam Frank takes aim at every ideology in sight, and its willingness to offend everyone equally makes it the most daring ticket Off-Broadway this fall.
I would much rather encounter a flawed, fearless piece of theatre that gives me something to wrestle with than another perfectly polished musical I have forgotten before reaching the subway.
During the 110 minutes of “Slam Frank”, you will be anything but bored.

“Slam Frank” mostly succeeds in satirizing the state of the mainstream American theater, which is inexplicably hell-bent on reimagining decades-old shows written by and for white people with BIPOC casts rather than supporting new work written by artists of diverse backgrounds.
The effort is admirable, but the satire is so even-handed that for most of the evening its point of view is nearly impossible to locate.
For most of the evening, Slam Frank effectively exposes the folly of reducing human experience to competing identities.

But any musical that opens with multiple projections of Patti LuPone for no apparent reason is out for easy laughs, and its program advisory, “Content Warning: Everything,” conveys what an exhausting experience this is.
Like many satires, ‘Slam Frank’ is too long, its punchlines too scattershot to sustain a nearly two-hour show Your response ultimately comes down to taste.
Such work is rare and hard and should be saluted (just not Nazi-style, please).
The way Slam Frank chooses to address it is quite possibly the most shocking thing I've ever seen in a New York theater.

cn.t: This audacious satire offends everyone equally with its hip-hop reimagining of Anne Frank, earning praise for its daring provocations and talented cast but criticism for muddled messaging and questionable taste.

vr.q: The show is funny. The show is subversive. The show is one of a kind and I think that is the reason to go see this.
I just wish it was shorter, I wish it was more focused, and I wish it actually committed to having something to say.
this final product still feels like it's throwing everything at the wall to see what sticks
